newsitem.title: USA: Political, environmental groups target Texaco.
newsitem.headline: Political, environmental groups target Texaco.

text.p: Less than two months after a federal judge approved a big settlement in a race discrimination case against Texaco Inc., the oil company is in for protests at its annual meeting over the environment and its presence in Burma.
Various groups said they plan to protest Texaco's environmental record in Ecuador, where they charge the company has polluted rivers and land and displaced Amazon indians.
In addition, Burmese political activists and a group led by the Rev. Jesse Jackson are planning to show up at Texaco Inc.'s annual meeting on Tuesday, protest groups said.

The Westchester People's Action Coalition, New York Student Environmental Coalition and Wetlands Environmental and Social Justice Centre said last week that they plan to stage protests outside the meeting, to be held in Rye Brook, N.Y.
The environmental activists said they are targeting Texaco's environmental record in Ecuador.

A lawsuit against the company has been rejected by a federal judge in White Plains, N.Y., but the case is being appealed by the government of Ecuador. Texaco is being sued for $800 million to $1 billion in the case for allegedly polluting rivers and land and displacing Amazon Indians.

Meanwhile, a student group called the Free Burma Coalition plans to stage a protest at the meeting over Texaco's stake in the Yetagun gas field in the Andaman Sea, 125 miles off the Burmese coast. Texaco owns a 42.9 percent stake.
Activists charge that U.S. companies that invest in Burma are prolonging the life of the country's military government.
Father Joe LaMar of the Interfaith Centre for Corporate Responsibilty said Texaco could avoid the disgrace suffered by another oil company involved in Burma, Unocal Corp., by pulling out now.

"They indicated to us that they were not necessarily committed to Burma. They can get out with a profit now," LaMar said. Texaco shareholders voted by a large margin at last year's annual meeting to reject calls to pull out of Burma.

Since then, the United States has imposed economic sanctions on new investment in Burma, and New York City and some state pension funds have said they may sell stakes in companies that do business or invest there.
Texaco has always said it will abide by U.S. law in its dealings in Burma.
Jesse Jackson is also expected to attend the meeting to protest Texaco's treatment of black employees, other groups said. His office could not be reached for comment.
Texaco in November agreed to pay $176.1 million to settle charges it discriminated against black employees, and a federal judge approved the settlement, the largest ever in such a case, on March 26.
But Texaco still faces charges from some critics that it has not done enough to treat minority employees fairly.
